title: 244. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Determining Domain from an Explicit Formula
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of a rational function by excluding values that make the denominator zero.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-5}\)?
questions.explanation: The function is defined only when the denominator is not zero. Set \(x-5\ne0\), which gives \(x\ne5\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(5\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find the value that makes the denominator zero and exclude it from the domain.

questions.concept: Domain of a Square Root Function
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of a square root function by requiring the radicand to be nonnegative.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-3}\)?
questions.explanation: For a square root to be defined over the real numbers, the radicand must be nonnegative. Thus \(x-3\ge0\), so \(x\ge3\). The value \(x=3\) is allowed because \(\sqrt{0}=0\). Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Set the expression inside the square root greater than or equal to zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Function with a Square Root in the Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain when a square root appears in the denominator.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-2}}\)?
questions.explanation:
The square root requires \(x-2\ge0\). The denominator also cannot be zero, so \(\sqrt{x-2}
e0\), which means \(x-2
e0\). Combining \(x-2\ge0\) with \(x-2
e0\) gives \(x-2>0\), so \(x>2\). Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: The denominator must be defined and must not be zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Quadratic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by excluding values that make a quadratic denominator zero.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-9}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). These values must be excluded. Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(3\) and \(-3\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and exclude each value that makes a factor zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Square Root Function with a Linear Radicand
questions.learningObjective: Solve a linear inequality to determine the domain of a square root function.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\sqrt{5-2x}\)?
questions.explanation: Require the radicand to be nonnegative: \(5-2x\ge0\). Subtract \(5\): \(-2x\ge-5\). Divide by \(-2\), reversing the inequality: \(x\le\frac{5}{2}\). Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: Remember to reverse the inequality sign when dividing by a negative number.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with an Always-Positive Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Recognize when a rational function has all real numbers as its domain.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\)?
questions.explanation: The denominator is \(x^2+1\). For every real number \(x\), \(x^2\ge0\), so \(x^2+1\ge1>0\). The denominator is never zero. Therefore the function is defined for all real numbers, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the denominator can ever equal zero.

questions.concept: Domain Combining a Square Root and a Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain when both a square root condition and a denominator restriction apply.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{x+4}}{x-1}\)?
questions.explanation:
The square root requires \(x+4\ge0\), so \(x\ge-4\). The denominator requires \(x-1
e0\), so \(x
e1\). The domain must satisfy both conditions. Therefore the domain is \(x\ge-4\) and \(x
e1\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find all restrictions separately, then keep only values that satisfy every restriction.

questions.concept: Domain of a Square Root Function with a Linear Radicand
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of a square root function by solving a linear inequality.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\sqrt{2x-6}\)?
questions.explanation: The radicand must be nonnegative: \(2x-6\ge0\). Add \(6\): \(2x\ge6\). Divide by \(2\): \(x\ge3\). The value \(x=3\) is allowed because the radicand becomes zero. Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Solve the inequality obtained by setting the radicand greater than or equal to zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Function with a Square Root in the Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by combining a radicand condition with a nonzero denominator condition.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}-2}\)?
questions.explanation:
The square root requires \(x+1\ge0\), so \(x\ge-1\). The denominator cannot be zero, so \(\sqrt{x+1}-2
e0\). Thus \(\sqrt{x+1}
e2\), which gives \(x+1
e4\), so \(x
e3\). Combining \(x\ge-1\) with \(x
e3\) gives the domain \(x\ge-1\) and \(x
e3\). Therefore option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find where the square root is defined, then exclude any value that makes the whole denominator zero.

questions.concept: Domain Combining a Square Root and a Rational Expression
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by combining a quadratic radicand condition with a denominator restriction.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{x^2-4}}{x-2}\)?
questions.explanation: The square root requires \(x^2-4\ge0\). Factoring gives \((x-2)(x+2)\ge0\), so \(x\le-2\) or \(x\ge2\). The denominator requires \(x-2\ne0\), so \(x\ne2\). Combining these conditions removes \(x=2\) from the interval \(x\ge2\), leaving \(x>2\). Therefore the domain is \(x\le-2\) or \(x>2\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Solve the radicand inequality first, then exclude any value that makes the denominator zero.
